topics.title: Support FluidEQ: GitHub Sponsors and Buy Me a Coffee
topics.body:
FluidEQ is free and open source, and it stays that way. If it earned a place in your setup and you'd like to help keep it going, there are two ways:

GitHub Sponsors: github.com/sponsors/StartSWest
Buy Me a Coffee: buymeacoffee.com/startswest, a one-off tip with no account needed.

The same two are behind the Support the work button in FluidEQ's title bar.
What support does, and doesn't

It supports the time that goes into FluidEQ: the engine, the fixes, the answers here.
It doesn't unlock anything. Everything in FluidEQ works the same with or without it, and it isn't a way to buy credits; those are separate, inside the app.
It doesn't buy a feature or a date. Ideas are weighed by votes in Ideas, for everyone the same.

Not in a position to give? Telling someone about FluidEQ, voting on ideas and reporting bugs help just as much.

topics.title: How the sound reaches your ears: the FluidEQ Engine and Equalizer APO
topics.body:
FluidEQ doesn't play your music; Windows does. To change the sound of everything the PC plays, FluidEQ puts an engine inside Windows' own audio. You choose which one, and one runs at a time.

The FluidEQ Engine (recommended)

Your sound card's own effects and its control panel keep working.
Your EQ and the DSP rack, the Room and the Game filter reach every app.
Each output keeps its own sound: headphones and speakers can be tuned completely differently.
It steps aside the moment FluidEQ quits, so an EQ never outlives the app.
While it runs, Equalizer APO is switched off and put back exactly as it was if you switch to it.

Equalizer APO

The open-source engine FluidEQ began on. It still ships inside the installer.
Choose it for custom APO commands, Peace or VST plugins.
It takes over your sound card's effect slot, so a vendor's panel can lose controls, and the DSP rack only plays in FluidEQ's Library.

Switching

Open the actions menu (≡) and press the engine card at the top.
Pick an engine and press Apply.
Windows asks for permission once, and the sound pauses for a few seconds while Windows audio restarts.

When an output says OFF, or nothing changes

OFF on an output: press Enable on its notice.
A notice says the engine isn't running: press Restart Windows audio.
Windows' Audio enhancements switched off for an output means Windows loads no engine there at all. FluidEQ says so and opens Windows' Sound page for you.
Still nothing, with everything looking right: Windows may be playing past the engine. The notice offers to move it to a place your sound card uses, for one permission prompt and a second of silence.

When an update brings a newer engine, a notice offers Update engine. An app update never swaps the engine on its own.
More in the app: Help → The FluidEQ Engine and When something sounds wrong. Still stuck: Something wrong? Where to report it.

topics.title: Scenes — the gallery and keeping a scene
topics.body:
This thread is for the Scenes tab.
What a scene is

A living picture under your EQ curves: mountains under the stars, aurora, a neon city, real 3D worlds.
Drawn on your graphics card and moving with your music; the bass, the beat and the treble each move something different.
The graph's forty standard looks and its measuring views are free and need no account.

The gallery

FluidEQ's own scenes and the ones members publish. Every published scene is reviewed before it appears.
Search, sort by Most liked, This week or Newest, or pick a category.
A scene with a preview loops a silent ten-second clip before you decide.

Keeping a scene

Get keeps it with one credit: yours for good, on every computer you sign in to, updating itself when its maker publishes a new version.
A new account starts with 3 free credits. More about credits: Accounts and the free credits.
Like the scenes you have with the heart, and report one that shouldn't be there.

Beyond the graph
A scene can play behind your desktop icons, and your RGB devices can take its colours. See The desktop background and Dynamic lighting.
Ask here about scenes, the gallery and credits.

topics.title: Welcome to FluidEQ — start here
topics.body:
I'm Ivan, and I make FluidEQ. This is the place for questions, ideas, tunings worth sharing, and anything behaving oddly.
What FluidEQ is

A system-wide equalizer and audio rack for Windows 10 and 11. Your EQ reaches everything the computer plays: games, browsers, music apps, calls.
Free and open source (GPL-3.0). The installer from fluideq.com and the Releases page is signed, and FluidEQ keeps itself up to date.
The sound needs no account. The equalizer, the DSP rack, the Room, the Library, Karaoke, the player, Share Audio and the graph's standard looks all work without ever signing up, and nothing is tracked.
An account is only for Scenes: the gallery, the Studio, the desktop background and Dynamic lighting. A new account gets 3 free credits, and each credit keeps a scene for good.

My Experience with FluidEQ
I met Ivan online, and since then we have exchanged several ideas about FluidEQ. It has been very interesting to follow the project’s development and see how much attention he gives to user feedback.
I am currently using version 1.6.1, and my experience so far has been very positive. The new internal DSP performs extremely well, even when playing Hi-Res music. On my system, FluidEQ uses approximately 500 MB of RAM while remaining smooth and stable.
The integration of the OPRA database, the native C++ DSP engine, and the ability to combine different forms of audio processing have turned FluidEQ into a very complete audio application. Although it started from AQUA and Equalizer APO, I believe it is already developing a strong identity of its own.
I also greatly appreciate Ivan’s willingness to listen to users, discuss suggestions, fix problems, and continuously improve the application. This kind of close relationship with the community is not something we always find in projects like this.
I hope to continue testing future versions, sharing suggestions, and contributing to the growth of this community. I recommend FluidEQ to anyone interested in equalization, DSP, and music playback on Windows. Give it a try and share your experience too!
Thank You, Ivan
Marco Maia

The desktop background

Puts a scene behind your desktop icons: on one monitor, or one on each.
Put a scene on the graph and press the monitor button beside its name, or choose View → Set as desktop background.

topics.title: Config — what the engine actually has on disk
topics.body:
This thread is for the Config tab.
What it's for: seeing what the engine actually has on disk — the FluidEQ Engine's or Equalizer APO's — not what FluidEQ intends. The two differ exactly when it matters: after a hand edit, another tool, or a restore from backup.
How it works: every layer is a file of its own, included per output, and the tab shows that include tree as it really is — what each file holds, which layers are on, and any include pointing at nothing. Each output also gets one file FluidEQ creates and never rewrites, applied last, for the commands that have no interface here; its filters are drawn on the graph and counted in the preamp. From here a whole chain exports to a .fluideq file and imports back onto the output you are listening to.
Ask here about the config layout, hand edits, and moving chains between machines.

topics.title: Outputs — every output its own sound, and a second output
topics.body:
This thread is for outputs.
What it's for: making the right sound follow the right device. Every setting belongs to the output you tuned it on — the EQ, the preset, the Tone, the DSP rack, the Room and the leveling — and comes back the moment you switch to it. Bluetooth headphones show their battery beside the output.
How it works: FluidEQ follows Windows' own ID for the device, not its name, so a rename or a re-plug changes nothing. A second output plays what you hear on other devices at the same time, each with its own sound and level; on the FluidEQ Engine it plays straight from the engine, and every delay is shown. Games can have a sound of their own too, under Game presets, switched when the game comes to the front and put back when it closes.
Ask here about outputs, profiles, the second output and game presets.

topics.title: The Room — surround on headphones
topics.body:
This thread is for the Room.
What it's for: turning headphones into a listening room. Every channel becomes a speaker standing around you: stereo is two speakers in front of you (or fills the room if you ask), a 5.1 film is five speakers and the sub, a 7.1 game the whole ring.
How it works: it is a stage of the DSP rack, heard through a measured head and the walls of a room. Twenty-four rooms to start from — eleven classics and thirteen newer ones — and everything a room is made of is on its page: where each speaker stands, how far, its level, the walls, the space and the bass management. A short listening test picks the head that puts sounds in front of you, by ear. All of it is free.
Ask here about rooms, the listening test, and surround from films and games.

topics.title: DSP — the studio rack
topics.body:
This thread is for the DSP tab.
What it's for: shaping the sound with a studio rack — eleven stages: Normalizer, Denoise, De-esser, Exciter, Bass Forge, Equaliser, Bass Punch, Dimension, Room, Maximizer and Master. Every stage starts off except the Normalizer, which only ever turns a hot record down.
How it works: on the FluidEQ Engine the rack runs on everything the computer plays. On Equalizer APO it applies to songs played in the Library only. Every stage draws what it is actually doing while it works, gain match takes added level back off so switching a stage compares the sound and not the volume, and Isolate plays only what a stage removes or adds. A whole rack saves, names and exports as a chain file, and the presets each bring a rack of their own.
Ask here about any stage, about chains, and about what the rack is doing to a record.

topics.title: Karaoke Maker — building the file when the song has none
topics.body:
This thread is for the Karaoke Maker.
What it's for: making the karaoke file when the song does not have one — from the song and nothing else.
How it works: it can first split the song into two tracks on your own machine: the backing track to sing over, and the voice, which is what the transcriber and the melody reader listen to. It takes well under a minute with a usable graphics card, about six without. The words can be transcribed from the audio or pasted in and kept. Timing is recorded by ear — mark each line as the track plays, then individual words where a line needs the detail. The melody is read off the recording into notes you can hear, split, retune, delete or add to by hand. Undo and redo run throughout, and the result goes straight to the player or saves as a project.
What it downloads, and only when you ask: a speech model to transcribe (about 570 MB, or 1.1 GB without a capable graphics card), a 361 MB pitch model to read the melody, and a 700 MB model to split the song. Each comes down once, on your press, never at launch, and your audio never leaves the machine. Pasting the words in, bringing your own instrumental, or timing by ear skips them.
Ask here about splitting, transcription, timing, the melody editor and project files.

topics.title: Karaoke — singing over your own files
topics.body:
This thread is for the Karaoke tab.
What it's for: singing over files you already own. Audio can be MP3, WAV, OGG, FLAC or M4A; lyrics can be .lrc for line timing, enhanced .lrc for word timing, or an UltraStar .txt for syllables and real target notes. Files sharing a name pair themselves into a playlist.
How it works: the words follow the audio's own clock, so a long song cannot drift away from them. Your microphone is chosen and switched on by you, analysed on your own machine, never recorded and never sent anywhere. The pitch lane draws target notes only when the file genuinely carries them, the chord guide names the chord now and the next one, and a review collects the places you sang high, low or missed and counts you back in. It goes full screen with the controls fading out of the way.
No music ships with it — the instrumental is one you already have, or one the Karaoke Maker splits out of the song itself (see its thread).

topics.body:
This thread is for the Online Media tab.
What it's for: something to tune against. YouTube, YouTube Music, Bandcamp, Twitch and Suno inside FluidEQ, with the response graph and live spectrum moving underneath.

topics.title: Convolution — impulse responses
topics.body:
This thread is for the Convolution tab.
What it's for: applying a measured impulse response ahead of everything else — verified minimum-phase responses from the AutoEq catalogue, searchable right in the tab by model or by who measured it, or any WAV of your own.
How it works: the file is analysed when it arrives, so the graph draws the response the file actually has rather than an approximation published beside it, and the preamp reserves against what it really does. A download matches the rate Windows runs your output at, and the FluidEQ Engine converts any other rate itself. It is a layer with its own switch, so hearing the chain without it is one press.
Ask here about impulse responses, importing your own WAVs, and what convolution is for in the first place.

topics.title: EQ Presets — headphone corrections from OPRA
topics.body:
This thread is for headphone corrections, your own curves and Squiglink.
What it's for: starting from a measurement instead of from scratch. 6,229 headphones and 12,594 published curves ship offline from OPRA, the community directory of headphone EQ profiles, grouped by brand and credited to whoever made them — AutoEq, oratory1990, Rtings.
How it works: a published correction is applied as a layer of its own, beside your bands, with its own strength and switch — so clearing your EQ does not throw it away. My curves is your own list beside OPRA's: curves from Squiglink, a .txt file, your EQ or an OPRA pick, each named, drawn and one press from playing, and the whole list exported or imported as one file. Squiglink has a tab of its own: export the EQ text there, paste it here, preview the curve, and apply it as editable bands or as a curve. The EQ mode card switches between corrections in one press.
The library updates on its own, and every release carries the current database with it. Every model also has a page on fluideq.com/headphones with its corrections drawn.
Ask here about corrections for your model, Squiglink imports and My curves.

My curves is your own list beside OPRA's: curves from Squiglink, a .txt file, your EQ or an OPRA pick, each named, drawn and one press from playing, and the whole list exported or imported as one file. Squiglink has a tab of its own: export the EQ text there, paste it here, preview the curve, and apply it as editable bands or as a curve. The EQ mode card switches between corrections in one press.

The library updates on its own, and every release carries the current database with it. Every model also has a page on fluideq.com/headphones with its corrections drawn.

Ask here about corrections for your model, Squiglink imports and My curves.

topics.body:
This thread is for the EQ tab — your own bands.
What it's for: the tuning you place by hand. Up to 128 bands per output, and every filter type there is — peak, low shelf, high shelf, low pass, high pass, band pass and notch — each with frequency, gain and Q. Any band can become one band per ear. Under the bands, the Tone row gives you Bass, Mid and Treble like an amplifier, with a low cut and a high cut either side.
How it works: your bands are one layer in the chain, with a switch of their own. The driver type, the headphone correction, the Tone, the preset and Smart EQ are separate layers, so clearing your bands never touches them, and every one of them can be switched off without being lost. Every layer feeds a single computed preamp: Auto normalize reserves headroom against the real combined response and against what the music actually needs, so stacking layers cannot clip you, and removing one gives the volume back. Everything belongs to the output you tuned it on — switch to your speakers and their sound comes back.
On the FluidEQ Engine the treble plays exactly as drawn up to 20 kHz, and every change crossfades instead of clicking; the EQ mode card lets you choose Equalizer APO's way of building the treble instead.
Ask here about bands, filter types, the Tone row, the preamp and Auto normalize. If the sound is wrong rather than the question, that is a bug — the issue tracker is the better place, so it does not get lost.
